meta.description: Not Bob Marley. Quote Investigator traces this line to country singer Roger Miller, who used it on a 1972 TV special — documented long before any Marley credit.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Some people feel the rain. Others just get wet'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bob Marley. The earliest documented use is Roger Miller on a 1972 ABC TV special; the Marley credit surfaced decades later with no source.

answer.label: Not Bob Marley — most likely Roger Miller
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Bob Marley ever said or wrote this. According to Quote Investigator, the earliest documented use is a review of Roger Miller’s ABC television special printed on 31 December 1972, and QI concludes Miller is “the most likely coiner.” The Bob Marley and Bob Dylan credits surfaced only decades later with no source in either man’s work.

source.heading: The earliest documented source

docMeta.dd: Roger Miller’s ABC television special (broadcast 1 Jan 1973)

source.excerpt: Some people feel the rain; others just get wet.
trail: Anchor: Quote Investigator finds the earliest instance in a 31 December 1972 Lubbock Avalanche-Journal review crediting Roger Miller, and repeated Roger Miller attributions through the 1970s.

By QI’s account, syndicated columnist Don Freeman of the San Diego Union ascribed the line to Miller on 21 December 1973 and again in 1978, and it appeared in Herb Cohen’s 1980 book You Can Negotiate Anything, all crediting Miller.
QI records the Bob Dylan credit only from 2007 and states it is “unlikely that Bob Dylan or Bob Marley crafted this expression” — the Marley credit has no early or sourced footing.
source.excerptNote: As quoted in a 31 December 1972 newspaper review of Roger Miller’s ABC television special, the earliest instance located by Quote Investigator.
source.rightsNote: The line is documented from a 1972 Roger Miller television performance — well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — so if credited to Miller it is in copyright to his estate. Because even Quote Investigator calls Miller only the “most likely” coiner, the precise authorship carries some uncertainty, but the post-1931 date rules out public domain either way.

author.name: Roger Miller
author.heading: Roger Miller
author.bio: Roger Dean Miller was an American singer-songwriter famous for novelty and story songs such as “King of the Road” and “Dang Me,” winning eleven Grammy Awards in the 1960s. Known for quick, folksy wit in the tradition of Will Rogers, he hosted television specials on which, per Quote Investigator, he used this exact line — the earliest documented use anywhere.

misattribution.heading: How Bob Marley got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “famous name” misattribution: a warm, aphoristic line drifts onto a beloved icon who never said it. Quote Investigator’s citation trail runs through Roger Miller, not Bob Marley.

items.why: Endlessly shared on Goodreads, memes and merchandise as Marley, but it appears in none of his songs, interviews or writings, and QI says it is “unlikely” he crafted it.
Also widely credited to Dylan, but QI finds this attribution only from 2007 — more than three decades after the line was already in print under Roger Miller’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented use ties the line to Roger Miller on a 1972 television special, per Quote Investigator — not Bob Marley or Bob Dylan.

context.heading: Why the line resonates
lead: The aphorism draws its punch from a simple reframe: the same rain falls on everyone, but attention turns a wet inconvenience into something felt and savored. That gentle, self-aware wit is exactly what made it a natural fit for Roger Miller’s television persona — and, later, an easy thing to pin on a reggae icon associated with sun, rain and easy wisdom.
context.pull: The same rain falls on everyone; only some people bother to feel it.
